title: Cardano Updates Feed
description: Regular updates from Cardano Development Teams

items.content_html:
High level summary​

  • Benchmarking: Node 11.2 release benchmarks; Dijkstra feature benchmarks: Nested Txns, reference script pricing, mempool / EB capacity; Leios Week45 benchmarks.
  • Development: Performance fixes for Node 11.2 closing space leak; locli analysis tool gets new major release 3.0.
  • Tracing: Correctness fixes for Tracing System; Alert manager ongoing work, currently focused on robust test harness.
  • Infrastructure: Dijkstra feature workloads along with tx-generator new major release 3.0 (draft PR); New workbench DuckDB/Parquet layer for compact, queryable logs (in testing); workbench maintenance.
  • Leios: Leios workload generator tx-centrifuge being equipped with Plutus workloads.
  • Node Diversity: Contributions to the London Workshop - Performance Observability Spec and workbench integration.

Low level overview​

Benchmarking​

The Performance & Tracing team has run, analyzed and published benchmarks for the Node 11.2 release. The full comparison against the 11.1 baseline, including our observations and conclusions, is available in the Performance report for 11.2.1.

In parallel, our performance workbench (the benchmarking automation framework) picked up a first round of benchmarks for upcoming Dijkstra-era features - nested transactions, reference script pricing, and mempool / EB (Endorser Block) capacity - to assess their performance characteristics ahead of any hard fork. The reference script results have been shared internally and are under discussion, while raw benchmark data for nested txns and mempool / EB capacity is still under analysis.

We've also continued our cluster benchmarks for Leios, this time on the Week45 build; we were able to empirically validate an important performance optimization, resulting in the certification of almost every EB, even when the network is under permanent, extreme submission pressure.

Development​

While working towards the Node 11.2 release in general, the team was also directly involved in closing two memory regressions. The more severe one had been flagged as a known issue since Node 11.1, with community complaints: writing a ledger snapshot no longer temporarily grows live memory by about the snapshot's own size, and the node's overall memory footprint drops markedly on top of that. See the Performance report for 11.2.1 for the full before/after picture. A second, smaller leak - introduced only in the 11.2.0 pre-release and caught before it reached anyone - retained part of the genesis ledger state for the node's entire lifetime; also fixed (ouroboros-consensus PR#2478).

Our analysis tool locli also reached a new major release, 3.0. It drops support for the legacy tracing formats that current node versions no longer emit, and its comparison reports are now Typst-only, so rendering a PDF no longer needs an Emacs/LaTeX toolchain. The release also adds new report sections for ledger snapshots and transaction processing, alongside a number of smaller metric fixes (cardano-node PR#6720).

Tracing​

November brought three correctness fixes across the tracing stack. A node could crash outright if an I/O error occurred while it was writing its own trace output to stdout - including while trying to print that very error - which is now guarded against (hermod-tracing PR#24). Separately, Hermod's Prometheus metrics server could end up permanently refusing a scraping host after a few socket timeouts, because an interrupted connection-close skipped releasing that host's reserved slot; the slot is now always released, even when the close itself is interrupted (hermod-tracing PR#29). And on cardano-node, a block producer could exit with status 1 on a clean, planned shutdown, because its ledger-metrics tracer kept querying the already-closed ChainDB; the tracer now runs in consensus's own resource registry, so it's cancelled before the ChainDB closes - this fix is currently under review (cardano-node PR#6782).

The monitoring/alarm system (cardano-node PR#6664) moved into its second phase in November: log-consumer dispatch now carries a rule's source, id, severity and summary rather than just a consumer name, and the timeseries producer gained a typed configuration and a pure, edge-triggered state machine (inactive / pending / active) with configurable "for" and "repeat every" windows and deterministic series keys. The evaluator thread and value decoding are left for a later iteration.

Last month's trace-filtering optimization work has since been validated and merged, for both Hermod and trace-dispatcher (hermod-tracing PR#27): dropping a filtered-out trace message is now roughly 5x cheaper in time and allocation, with no measurable difference for cardano-node itself, whose own trace volume is too low for the saving to show up.

Infrastructure​

Our performance workbench is getting tx-generator ready for the Dijkstra era: a new major release, 3.0, adds a generator for nested transactions - transactions that themselves carry sub-transactions - script variants and reference scripts for Plutus workloads (so the ledger's script-decoding cache can't hide their true cost), and support for Plutus V4 (cardano-node PR#6776). Transactions are now built through cardano-api's new Compatible interface rather than the deprecated functions it replaces. The PR is currently under review.

Separately, the workbench gained a new DuckDB/Parquet layer for its logs, still in testing (cardano-node feature branch): a run's node, generator and explorer logs are converted once into compact Parquet files, queryable directly with SQL via DuckDB instead of being re-parsed from raw text for every analysis. Beyond faster, ad-hoc queries for our own analysts, it also lets us cross-check locli's own metrics independently over the same data, and query a remote run's logs over SSH without copying them off the benchmark host first.

A smaller workbench maintenance PR has been merged (cardano-node PR#6764): safer handling of a run's metadata (no more silently truncated or placeholder-filled manifests on a fetch), a configurable override for the ledger-snapshot schedule, and a new 6-dense profile family on Protocol Version 10.

Leios​

Our Leios workload generator tx-centrifuge is being equipped with Plutus workloads, catching up to what tx-generator already offers for Praos benchmarks. The goal is to measure the performance impact of different execution-budget limits for EBs - how tightly such a limit can be set before it starts constraining throughput. This is still early-stage work, with no branch yet to point to.

Node Diversity​

At the London Workshop, ICAN's CEO presented the team's work on a Cardano node performance observability specification (cardano-node branch). The branch holds two companion documents. The first specifies which events any Cardano node implementation - not only the Haskell one - has to emit so its performance can be analyzed by our workbench and compared against other implementations under the same workload: for each event, the precise moment it marks and what its payload means, grouped into conformance tiers so an implementation can start with the essentials (block production, diffusion, resource usage) and add detail later. The second document covers everything else a node needs to take part in a workbench benchmark run: delivery as a self-contained executable, a fixed invocation with no node-specific flags from the workbench, and a clearly bounded, self-declared footprint in cores and memory.

Together, the two documents are meant to give the ecosystem one yardstick for all node implementations - a precise, implementation-agnostic way to measure and compare performance across different Cardano clients.
items.title: Performance & Tracing Update

items.content_html:
High level summary​

We continued with Leios work this cycle, with most of the work going into the endorser block and the block header. The endorser block rule gained its real validations, moving it past the placeholder check it started out with. The Leios header hash was corrected so that it covers only the header body and the KES signature. Forecasting was extended with the maximum transaction size, which Leios is the first protocol to have a reason to forecast, and the block header coders were brought back.

CIP-172, self-usable transaction outputs, was implemented, reaching across the Babbage, Conway and Dijkstra eras.

Two protocol-level safety fixes landed. Governance updates that would set the maximum pledge leverage below one are now rejected, since such a value can produce negative pool rewards and abort reward application entirely. Separately, a change to the VRF duplicate counter that had accidentally altered Conway behavior while fixing Dijkstra was reverted, the two code paths having turned out not to be equivalent.

Sub-transaction support was rounded out on the API side. The helper reporting the outputs a transaction produces now includes sub-transaction outputs, where a batch creating three UTxOs previously reported only the top-level one. The timelock upgrade function was also fixed and renamed.

Testing was dominated by Plutus V4 and by conformance. The V4 transaction info translation, which had been merged without unit tests, received a thorough set covering each translated field. The Plutus script decoder is now checked to agree with the Plutus deserializer across every language, PLC version, protocol version and builtin. A transaction-level guard script exercises batch validation, including the phase-2-invalid cases. The formal ledger specification was updated three times over the cycle, each time enabling further tests, and the maximum pool stake calculation is now property-tested against the specification.

Tooling gained a custom git diff driver for CBOR files, wired up automatically through the development shell, so binary CBOR now shows up as readable text in diffs.

Low level summary​

Features​

  • PR-6268 - EB rule validations
  • PR-6287 - Hash only header body and signature

  • PR-6277 - Reject maximum pledge leverage updates below one
  • PR-6300 - Revert previous behavior of VRF duplicates counter initialization

High level overview​

The team kept working on the discovery of the facts of the Cardano node, the guessing of the Mithril signer and DMQ node parameters and the terminal user interface of the setup command, and the assessment of the impact of the client Kubo node acting as an IPFS peer. items.title: Mithril Team Update

items.content_html:
High level summary​

  • Leios implementation on main (Treasury Funding Initiative 4: Ouroboros Leios Implementation):
    • The LeiosDB now stores each endorser block as one row per point, with its body and transactions as stored bytes. Before, it wrote two rows per transaction, so a full endorser block touched tens of thousands of rows (#2424).
    • The LeiosFetch server now sends an endorser block as the bytes that it stored, without a decode. This changes the wire format of MsgLeiosBlock (#2495).
    • The port of the fetch logic from the prototype continues. We added the pure decision logic of LeiosFetch (#2491) and the interface that tells other node components when an endorser block arrives (#2521).
    • The limits on the age of the announcements that a node relays or accepts are now configurable. Test networks need smaller limits, because their immutable tip is only minutes old (#2489).
    • The node now aggregates the votes that it relays into a certificate when they reach quorum. It traces each announcement that misses quorum by its deadline (#2459).
    • The mempool reserves room for an endorser block only when the Leios committee has enough stake with registered voting keys. Until then, the mempool behaves as it does in Praos (#2482, and #2481 for the prototype).
  • Leios prototype (Treasury Funding Initiative 4: Ouroboros Leios Implementation):
    • A second version of adaptive endorsements. If an endorser block misses its quorum, block producers make the next ones smaller. Each endorser block that reaches its quorum adds a small amount of capacity back (#2480).
    • The fetch client now writes to the LeiosDB synchronously, which removes a class of race conditions. Block producers no longer fetch their own endorser blocks from peers (#2477).
    • We fixed a memory spike in the LeiosNotify server (#2500).
  • Maintenance and support (Treasury Funding Initiative 17: Maintenance and Support):
    • Released ouroboros-consensus 5.4.0.0 with support for the new ledger release (#2487).
    • Released ouroboros-consensus 5.4.0.1. In this release, the LSM backend no longer counts its wait time as IOWAIT, so node metrics show the real disk wait (#2518, #2519).
items.title: Consensus Team Update

items.content_html:
Overview​

Summary​

Ouroboros-Network​

We released network-mux-0.12.0.0, ouroboros-network-1.3.0.0 and cardano-diffusion-1.3.0.0, followed by the ouroboros-network 2.0 release, which dmq-node has already adopted. cardano-diffusion 1.1.0.0 and 1.1.1.0 were released earlier.

Tx-submission. The V2 tx-submission without a central decision thread was merged. Since then we fixed duplicate txids in the outbound side, fixed truncated duration counters (waits shorter than a millisecond were counted as zero), switched outbound calculations to Int, and made awaitSharedChange an STM action so dmq-node can resolve races in a single transaction. NodeToNodeV_16 with configurable tx-submission limits was merged. Bounding the work done during a sweep (at most 1000 entries per STM transaction) is in progress.

Network-mux. Mux SDU header encoding/decoding is now about 70% faster and allocates over 90% less. The mux now forces the first 256 KiB of a message in the sender's thread, so an unevaluated encoding waiting in the egress buffer no longer retains whatever it refers to. Mux counters were added, enabling per-mini-protocol dashboards. Fixes to mux timeouts (cancelling timeouts when actions throw and keeping timeout monitors cancellable under masking) are in review, and an RTT-aware mux using echo-cookie RTT sampling is being prototyped. Work has started on a mux egress scheduler, which serves bearers by tiers and tracks egress counters and busy periods, alongside batching changes in the mux (withBatch, GrantAt).

Connection manager & inbound governor. Several race conditions were fixed: connection-manager / inbound-governor races (including a connection leak), a race on new connections in the inbound governor (with a new IOSimPOR test), and the inbound governor no longer blocks on a stale MuxFinished. Two small memory leaks were fixed, in the KeepAlive server and in cardano-node's acceptAcceptor. The diffusion layer now filters configured or negotiated mini-protocols before passing them to the mux.

Peer selection. Peers whose peer-share request failed are now backed off (default 1 hour), and the peer-share time is only updated for peers we are still connected to. Topology reload of local roots given as IP addresses is fixed (previously they waited for DNS-named local roots, never updating when there were none). DNS TTL handling was fixed, and upstreamyness tracing was added, also reducing the likelihood of immediately re-promoting hot peers. We also added a Hashable API, and work on running diffusion on multiple network interfaces is in review.

Ping. The ping API for validating SRV records / registration certificates was merged, to be used by cardano-cli, together with output formatting improvements; further output improvements are in review.

Window-stats. A new window-stats library provides efficient rolling-window statistics backed by a finger tree — a first step towards exposing connection metrics to applications. It already powers the Leios percentile metrics in cardano-node. Follow-ups include API changes, renaming and an insert performance fix.

Smol-world. We are building smol-world, a discrete-event simulator with a realistic transport model (loss, RFC 6298 RTO, CUBIC congestion control per RFC 9438) on a small-world topology with per-node egress contention, to study diffusion at scale. TCP model refinements are in review.

Leios​

The improved ΔQ analysis of Linear Leios EB diffusion was merged. It fixes three bugs in the earlier model, sweeps over EB closure sizes to determine practical limits, and analyses the sensitivity to mempool fragmentation (1-hop vs. multi-hop closure fetch, TxCache miss rate). We also published the incremental decoding benchmark results in the Leios design document. In cardano-node we added CDFs of EB announcement delays (with a follow-up fix) and fixed the Praos CDF; replacing the CDFs with p90/p95/p99 percentiles is in review.

We are also experimenting with a whole-closure store-and-forward EB fetch policy with bounded hedging in ouroboros-consensus: a peer offers a closure only once it holds all of it, receivers request only the missing transactions, and RTT-aware deadlines trigger hedged requests to alternative suppliers when progress stalls. In a 64-node cardano-ignite experiment it reduced median time for a closure to reach all nodes from 5.6 s to 4.1 s, and cut redundant closure payload from 86 MB to 1 MB (amplification 1.53× → 1.01×).

DMQ-Node​

We released dmq-node-0.7.0.0 (ouroboros-consensus-4.0, ouroboros-network-1.2, GHC-9.14 support) and dmq-node-0.7.2.0, and updated to ouroboros-network-2.0 and ouroboros-consensus-5.2. Integration for Node release 11.1 was completed. Other changes include peer-sharing timeouts and an explicit CBOR decode error for local message notification, changes to the signature outbound side, lowering the minimum signature body size to 90 bytes, an internal --min-sig-delay flag, a custom validation config fix, and running Hydra CI on aarch64-linux.

IOSim, io-classes & typed-protocols​

io-classes-1.11 and typed-protocols-1.2.2.0 were released. An io-sim performance fix (reverting eager evaluation of say/traceM/traceSTM arguments) was merged, and ppSayTrace was added. A fix for timeout raising a stale exception after it returned and a TimeDuration type class are in review. IOSimPOR gained finer control over which threads take part in schedule exploration (explorationRacyByLabel, with labelled fork/async variants); this is in review.

items.title: Network Team Update

items.content_html:
High level summary​

We continued to focus on Leios this cycle, with the endorser block moving from a data definition to something the ledger can actually validate and apply. The EB and EBLEDGERS rules were implemented, a Leios certificate validation API was exposed from the ledger API, and endorser block application arrived through applyEndorserBlock. Endorser block references were made era-parametric, so they are no longer pinned to a single era. On the pool side, updates that only touch BLS keys no longer require owner witnesses, closing a gap that would have forced unnecessary signatures on key rotation.

Dijkstra gained a distinct mempool transaction representation, separating what the mempool carries from the transaction type used elsewhere. Plutus V4 scripts are now evaluated against the actual V4 API rather than borrowing the previous version's. The state-annotated transaction now also carries reference script size and execution units, so the rules no longer recompute them on every use.

The reference input cost parameter for multi-assets was renamed and retyped, moving from a per-policy to a per-byte cost. Per-policy pricing could not be made fair, since a single policy may carry arbitrarily many asset names, whereas the binary overhead of a multi-asset is straightforward to compute directly.

Testing concentrated on conformance and on the new endorser block machinery. Conformance now tracks which tests are expected to fail, so a disabled test that starts passing is no longer silently ignored, and the tests that already passed were re-enabled. A property test for top-level transaction info was added, comparing the aggregated result against a reference implementation built field by field across the nested transactions of a batch.

Low level summary​

Features​

  • PR-6216 - Leios certificate validation API
  • PR-6215 - Add EB and EBLEDGERS
  • PR-6248 - Add DijkstraApplyBlock with applyEndorserBlock
  • PR-6241 - Make EbReferences era parametric
  • PR-6217 - Do not require owners to witness updates for BLS keys
  • PR-6257 - Introduce BlockEnv for ApplyBlock

items.content_html:
High level overview​

This week, the Mithril team resolved the SNARK verification key collisions deterministically in the key registration, measured the download time of a mainnet Cardano database with IPFS on dev-mainnet, and implemented a ratio for IPFS downloads in the client. They also filled the fake protocol configuration reader from a JSON hex-encoded marker configuration.

The team kept working on the activation of the snark feature by default, the prototype of the orchestrator of the setup command, the migration of the existing immutable archives to the deterministic format, and the stabilization of the certificate chain cache in the client library and CLI.

Finally, they replaced the retired macos-14 runner in the CI workflows, and worked on the upgrade to Cardano node 11.2 and on the size of the signature messages sent to the DMQ node.

Low level overview​

items.content_html:
High level summary​

The Plutus team has continued work on the Dijkstra builtins and conformance testing. In particular we've finalized the cost models of the keepPolicies and dropPolicies builtins (CIP-0168). We've also added 65 conformance cases for the new Value builtins, and specified these builtins and multiIndexArray in the Plutus Core specification.

On the metatheory front, a new tool generates Agda typechecking tests from the conformance suite. We've also added the new builtins to the metatheory as postulates, and added support for casing on Data to the certifier's case-reduce pass.

Other than these, we've fixed the PIR and UPLC constant folding passes so they no longer fold builtin applications with impure arguments, which could incorrectly discard computations that fail. We've also fixed compilation of Plutus V4 context types and aligned the lookupCoin and valueContains memory models with the existing cost-model parameters.

Work in progress includes implementing arrays and bytestrings in the metatheory, fixing certification of the case-of-case pass, and further CEK machine optimizations.

items.title: Plutus Core Team Update

items.content_html:
High level summary​

  • Leios implementation on main (Treasury Funding Initiative 4: Ouroboros Leios Implementation):
    • In the Dijkstra era, block producers now forge endorser blocks from the transactions that do not fit in the ranking block, and write them to the LeiosDB (#2377, #2442).
    • The ChainDB now opens the LeiosDB and drives its garbage collection (#2431). The LeiosDB no longer de-duplicates transactions, which makes its schema simpler (#2370).
    • Chain selection now checks the Leios certificate of a block when the block arrives. It waits to select the block until the node has the certified endorser block (#2439, #2433).
    • The node now relays Leios votes. It checks each vote once and disconnects from a peer that sends an invalid vote (#2430).
    • The Leios decoders now reject oversized hashes and endorser blocks. This ports the fix for audit finding LEI-004 from the prototype (#2440, #2458).
    • The LeiosDB benchmark now measures latency under load instead of throughput (#2422).
  • Leios prototype (Treasury Funding Initiative 4: Ouroboros Leios Implementation):
    • Released rc-2026w43. The LeiosDB writes endorser blocks faster, and block producers forge certifying blocks in milliseconds instead of up to 0.9 s (#2449, #2451).
    • Released rc-2026w44 with adaptive endorsements. If endorser blocks do not get enough votes, block producers forge smaller ones, so throughput goes down step by step instead of falling back to Praos levels (#2475, ouroboros-leios#1152).
    • The node now traces the time and cost to validate an endorser block, for our performance models (#2443).
  • Maintenance and support (Treasury Funding Initiative 17: Maintenance and Support):
    • Released ouroboros-consensus 5.3.0.0 (#2470). It lowers memory use when the node writes ledger snapshots (#2467, #2468). The forging traces no longer count the mempool snapshot time as block forging time (#2471).
    • cardano-node no longer reports a false configuration difference for the default LSM database path (cardano-node#6742).
items.title: Consensus Team Update

items.content_html:
High level summary​

  • Benchmarking: Preliminary benchmarks on the Leios prototype and the Leios Week42 build; refinement of performance analysis.
  • Development: In preparation for Node 11.2, we focused on fixing issues and addressing reports from the community.
  • Tracing: Switch to Hermod Tracing - preparation phase concluded; Optimization pass for trace filtering; Alert manager and Native spans ongoing.
  • Infrastructure: New Dijkstra-scoped benchmarks such as nested transactions and reference script measurements.
  • Leios: Tx validation benchmark on SPO hardware analyzed.

Low level overview​

Benchmarking​

The Performance & Tracing team has done several cluster benchmarks on the Leios prototype and the subsequent Leios Week42 build. There were several focus areas we watched out for, such as the ratio of certified EBs (Endorser Blocks). With voting traffic and timing constraints, and physical bandwidth being known limiting factors, we wanted to measure both high- and low-confidence parameter sets for the protocol in that regard. Additionally, we compared RBs' (Ranking Blocks') performance properties to a Praos-only baseline - how do block production, diffusion and adoption metrics fare? Then, we quantified mempool fragmentation and potential improvements due to the TxCache. Last but not least, as usual, our eye was on resource usage of a fully integrated build.

Our surgical windows into Leios performance are still being adjusted, based on the observations we make and asks from the Leios team; we're continuously refining coverage of our performance reports for Leios. All of the findings have been shared with the Leios team; however, they're not a public item as they do not describe an official release candidate and already contain known bottlenecks that are actively being worked on.

Development​

In preparation for Node 11.2, the team worked through a handful of community-reported bugs. A counter tracking slots missed while block forging was intentionally disabled used to jump by the whole disabled interval the moment forging resumed, booking time that was never actually missed; this is now fixed (cardano-node PR#6726). On Windows - and on Linux under a non-UTF-8 locale - the node could crash outright on a non-ASCII host or node name, or emit trace lines that weren't valid UTF-8; both cardano-node and cardano-tracer now force UTF-8 console encoding on startup regardless of the host's locale settings (cardano-node PR#6731). On the Hermod Tracing side, the Prometheus metrics endpoint now exposes its label sets with full conformance to the Prometheus text format, fixing a parsing issue some scrapers ran into (hermod-tracing PR#20).

Tracing​

As reported in earlier posts, the plan is to replace the node's current tracing system (trace-dispatcher) with Hermod Tracing once it's ready, bringing a cleaner API/core split, live reconfiguration of trace filter rules, and a single source of truth for defining tracers used across emission, documentation and consistency checks. Hermod Tracing's packages have now reached version 1.1.0, completing the API rework needed so the node's own dependencies - ouroboros-network, cardano-diffusion and ouroboros-consensus - can build against Hermod's lightweight public interface alone, rather than pulling in the full implementation package (hermod-tracing PR#21). With this now tested together with the existing node codebase, the preparation phase for the tracing system switch is concluded.

Separately, the team has been making the cost of a filtered-out trace message as cheap as possible, since most emitted traces are dropped by a severity or namespace filter before they're ever written anywhere. A series of changes to Hermod's internal configuration and message-combination logic - avoiding repeated allocations, building configured tracers once instead of per message, and specialising hot code paths - cut the cost of discarding such a message by roughly 7x, with a similar drop in memory allocated per message (hermod-tracing feature branch). The work isn't in a PR yet, pending full validation.

The monitoring/alarm system (cardano-node PR#6664) as well as library support of tracing spans (hermod-tracing PR#19) is ongoing work, with the latter being finalized and under review currently.

Infrastructure​

In preparation for the Node 11.2 release, the team extended our performance workbench (the benchmarking automation framework) with new Dijkstra-scoped profiles: nested transactions - transactions that themselves carry sub-transactions - and reference-script-based Plutus calls, benchmarked alongside the existing witness-script path (cardano-node feature branch). Getting representative results for the nested-transaction profiles also required lowering how long a node waits before requesting transactions from a newly connected peer, from the default 60 seconds down to 1, so the new profiles' load reaches the whole cluster fast enough to produce meaningful numbers.

Leios​

Validating that Leios's ledger-side assumptions hold up on a real implementation is an effort we've reported on over several past posts: can the ledger keep up with the transaction throughput Leios is designed for, and - since that depends heavily on disk I/O once the UTxO set no longer fits in memory - how much does storage hardware matter (Leios issue#553)? Last month we turned the resulting transaction-validation benchmark into a standalone executable and shipped it to SPOs so it could be run directly on their own hardware, without a nix or Haskell/cabal stack.

We've now collected and analysed submissions from a broad sample of real SPO machines. Raw read latency per transaction varied by about 32x across the field; once that's adjusted for each machine's raw CPU speed (which accounts for much of the spread on its own), the gap narrows to roughly 7-8x, driven mainly by one factor: whether a disk's write cache is write-back or write-through. Write-through disks were close to 6x slower than write-back ones before adjusting for CPU, and still more than 3x slower after - unless they sit behind a battery-backed RAID controller, which closes most of the gap. The full breakdown is available for anyone who wants to dig deeper (Benchmark results).

items.content_html:
High level summary​

Leios remained the main focus and moved further toward its concrete block and certificate structure. We added the LEIOSCERT rule together with the Leios-certificate-related BBODY failures, defined the EbReferences CDDL and an Annotator decoder for it, and started tracking the last tick slot number in the new epoch state and the last endorser block announcement in the ledger state. We also prevented duplicate BLS keys from being used, improved how Leios committee seats are rendered (hex keys and decimal weights), integrated the week 42 ledger changes on the prototype branch, and backed the work with Leios certificate golden tests and better example parameters.

A significant milestone was the Dijkstra era gaining its economic machinery: we implemented the minFee calculation for Dijkstra, adopted the CIP-23 effective cost and margin in the rewards calculations, and fixed the block body size computation. There was also a cluster of serialisation and decoder fixes, covering the PlutusData decoder, redeemers for protocol version 12, NonEmpty set and map decoders, and the IPv4 encoding order (now network order rather than swapped), with property tests added for Plutus data conversion.

Work on sub-transactions continued, with min-ada validation switched to a non-static check and submitTx in the ImpTests now randomly exercising top-level and sub-level transactions, alongside new Imp tests for SUBDELEG, SUBPOOL and SUBGOVCERT. On the rules side we added LEDGER rule limits and stopped inverting predicate failures in the small-steps framework, and we simplified transaction hashing by removing hashTx and the DijkstraEraTx type class in favour of the existing HashAnnotated. We also added a queryStakePoolState ledger state query.

On the testing and releasing side we enabled ExUnits tests and fixed the bootstrap witness in conformance, made the Plutus tests run with arbitrary Plutus versions, added tests for transValidityInterval and for the ValidityInterval/VotingProcedures semigroup and monoid instances, tested voting stake computation for pools with zero delegations, updated the formal ledger specification, and filled in a few missing predicate-check ImpTests. Infrastructure changes were limited to a cleret bump to 0.5.2.1 and a dependency update.

items.title: Plutus Core Team Update

items.content_html:
High level summary​

  • Leios implementation on main (Treasury Funding Initiative 4: Ouroboros Leios Implementation):
    • Merged the Praos2 protocol into main. Praos2 is Praos plus the Leios overlay. One definition, PolyPraos, now has all the Praos rules, and both Praos and Praos2 are variants of it. When a later Praos variant comes, it will extend PolyPraos instead of adding a new protocol next to it (#2386). A follow-up fixes the translation of the LedgerView from Conway to Dijkstra, a defect that #2386 kept from the old code (#2399).
    • An Endorser Block can no longer get its certificate in a later era or a later epoch than the block that announced it. The era rule avoids open design questions about a block that crosses an era boundary. The epoch rule keeps the interface between consensus and the ledger simpler (#2409).
    • Moved the LeiosNotify clients from the leios-prototype branch to main. A client disconnects from a peer that sends a message that an honest node would not send. A new test suite runs the real node against peers that can send any message (#2403).
    • Moved the LeiosFetch servers from the leios-prototype branch to main (#2416). The next step is the logic that decides which Endorser Blocks to fetch, and the clients that fetch them.
    • Fixed a defect in the LeiosDB garbage collection. If an exception stopped a collection pass, the rows that the pass marked for deletion stayed in the database. The next pass now finds and deletes them (#2401).
    • The Leios design document now has a detailed section on Endorser Block diffusion. It gives the plan that came out of the LeiosFetch design work, and how the node keeps its memory use bounded (ouroboros-leios#1005).
  • Leios prototype development (Treasury Funding Initiative 4: Ouroboros Leios Implementation):
    • Merged a large change that makes Endorser Block diffusion in the prototype close to the production design (#2282). Some examples:
      • The node fetches an Endorser Block only when an election or a certificate justifies it, never because a peer offers it.
      • A peer can offer only an Endorser Block that it announced, and each part only once. If a peer breaks a rule, the node disconnects from it.
      • If an announcement gives the wrong size for an Endorser Block, the node does not relay that block and does not vote for it.
      • The node checks the certificate in a ranking block when the block arrives, before chain selection.
    • Before #2282, the prototype used the Leios header format in all eras. It now uses the Leios format from Dijkstra only, and the unchanged Praos format before. The testnet starts before Dijkstra, so we must restart its chain from genesis, and every node must update.
    • LeiosNotify has two new messages, MsgQuit and MsgCanceled, so the node can stop a session while it waits for a reply. Before, this was not possible. So when the peer governor moved a peer from hot to warm, the node closed the whole connection (#2344).
    • Backported the epoch rule from #2409 to the prototype (#2415).
  • Maintenance and support (Treasury Funding Initiative 17: Maintenance and Support):
    • Released ouroboros-consensus 5.1.0.1. The tool db-truncater has a new flag, --leios. Without the flag, the tool does not need the LeiosDB files and does not change them (#2393).
    • Tracing now shows the Dijkstra ledger predicate failures. Before, the log formatting for these failures called error, so a Dijkstra block that failed validation crashed the thread that wrote the trace (#2406, ported to main in #2407).
    • Added the local state query GetStakePoolState, which the ledger defines in cardano-ledger#6162 (#2412, for #2405).
    • Added golden tests for the ledger queries. They catch a change to the encoding of a query or its result, which would break client tools. Queries that the ledger already defines, such as NonMyopicMemberRewards, now come from the ledger (#2348).
    • A ledger snapshot now has one version number at the top level, instead of one number for each part. New tests check the golden snapshot files against the CDDL specification, which catches an encoding that does not match the specification. This change also fixes the Peras CDDL (#2395).
    • db-synthesizer now uses the forge function and the mempool of the node, instead of its own copy of the forging logic. One visible change: every slot leader now forges a block, so the synthesized chain can have forks (#2284).

items.content_html:
High level summary​

Leios continued to be the main focus this cycle and moved well beyond prototype on several fronts. Dijkstra forecasting for Leios landed, the forecasting itself was simplified by keeping stake data only in snapshots, and DijkstraEraForecast was extended with the Peras protocol parameters. We defined Leios' EndorserBlock, added a ledger state query for the Leios committee, switched the Leios header KES signature verification to use MemoBytes, and fixed pool BLS key handling so the key's epoch number is only renewed when the key is actually new. These were backed by tests for the Leios committee and stake distribution when injecting genesis data, and by integration of the latest Leios changes for week 41.

PlutusV4 reached a milestone for the Dijkstra era: eraMaxLanguage is now set to PlutusV4, and AlonzoTxWits encodes and decodes PlutusV4 scripts starting with Dijkstra. Work on sub-transactions continued, with allInputsTxBodyF now looking into sub-transactions, top-level supplemental datums allowed for sub-transactions, and tests added for refunds in the consumed value across a batch. On the Dijkstra era more broadly, we fixed VRF reuse at the epoch boundary, started tracking the VRF key hashes of genesis stake pools, moved NonMyopicMemberRewards into the ledger, added missing getters to AnyEraTxBody, and renamed requiredTopLevelGuardsL while bringing in its outstanding tests.

On testing and releasing we added further Entities tests, treasury value and reference-script size tests, enabled bootstrap addresses in conformance, updated the formal ledger specification, and bumped the Plinth version in the Plutus preprocessor modules. Infrastructure changes included a cardano-data changelog fix for the pointWise to pointwise rename, a round of package version bumps across the changelogs following a CHaP release, and the usual dependency bump.

items.content_html:
High level overview​

This week, the Mithril team completed adding a Proof of Bound Possession for the SNARK verification keys, renaming the future_snark feature to snark, adding the missing conversion and error-path tests in IVC SNARK, and testing the SNARK infrastructure to full security parameters with the Midnight fix. They kept working on hardening the SNARK primitives.

The team completed adding an IndexedDB backend for the certificate chain cache in the WASM client and documenting the certificate chain cache, fixed the IPFS end to end tests failing when dist.ipfs.tech is unreachable, and fixed the crates publication dry run failing in the nightly. They also worked on the new distribution release, the upgrades to Cardano node 11.1.3 and 11.2, the update of the DMQ node to 0.7.2.0, a keypair generation tool in the aggregator CLI, and kept investigating the blocks and transactions verification failure on the testing-preview network.

Finally, they completed the upgrade to Rust 1.99, and fixed the missing SPO aliases in the explorer, the flakiness of the end to end tests caused by the devnet scripts, and the cloud uploader cache which only held the first 1000 files.
